kolu under any chat app

Comparisons·seedling·proposed·JUL 13, 2026

The coding agent has moved into the chat. kolu is the open, model-agnostic terminal/file foundation any chat app integrates — and the model is a mirror of the coordinator: observe flows out raw (the who-needs-me board), act flows in through one disciplined orchestrator agent, and the same door makes the coordinator a grounded participant in the humans' own discussion. The first proof is an XS bot binding a thread to the coordinator that already runs kolu's own development.

A read of Anthropic’s Claude Tag (Claude joins the team chat as a tagged teammate) and AI researcher Andrej Karpathy’s framing of it as “the 3rd major redesign of LLM UIUX,” held against what kolu is. Throughout, XS stands for any chat app (a Slack-style team chat where the agents already live), and pesu (Tamil பேசு, “to speak”) is a minimal XS bot — the first thing to run kolu’s own development inside chat.

The short version

kolu is the foundation a chat app integrates — it runs real terminals on machines you control and watches what happens inside them. kolu runs claude, codex, or opencode under any front end, on infrastructure you own. The integration is a mirror of the coordinator: observing comes straight off the daemons (the who-needs-me board), and acting goes through one door — an orchestrator agent in an ordinary kolu terminal. XS — the chat app — keeps everything social: identity, login, presence, attribution. kolu authenticates nothing; the connection is the trust.

The shift: the agent moved into the chat

Karpathy isn’t describing a chatbot you ask questions. He’s describing a coworker: a persistent agent that lives where the team already works, holds the org’s tools and context, and runs tasks on its own while you do something else. You @-tag it, walk away, and it pings you when it needs you. Anthropic shipped this shape as Claude Tag — one shared Claude per channel, tasks it pursues “over hours or days,” an audit log of every task and who asked for it. The proof-point is blunt: “65% of our product team’s code is created by our internal version.” The work moves into chat, and the human’s job shifts from driving keystrokes to managing agents.

In that world the terminal specializes. Chat keeps gaining richer rendering — diffs, highlighting, even little editors — but it stays async text over request and response. It is not a live process you can step into. The terminal is where you drop to a shell, answer an interactive prompt, watch raw output, drive a debugger. Chat owns the breadth; the terminal owns the depth — and kolu is what makes the depth real.

kolu in one picture

At its core kolu does two things: it runs real terminals on computers you control, and watches what’s happening inside them. That core is three parts:

  • kaval owns each live terminal — start an agent, type into it, resize it, kill it. It is also the single point that serializes writes: when input arrives, last one wins.
  • padi is the per-host workspace daemon above it: its agent sensors watch every terminal without touching it, folding the raw noise into a simple board — which agent is working, which is asking you something, which just finished — and it owns the durable session: what each terminal ran, the agent’s resume identity, restore across restarts and even an unclean daemon death.
  • @kolu/surface is the typed wire that carries both over any connection — a local socket, or ssh to another machine. Remote hosts are a shipped, first-class part of the app: add a host and its terminals sit behind a host switcher, on desktop and mobile.

Two things sit either side of kolu, and the relationship with each is different:

  • XS is independent. It already runs without kolu. Integrating kolu is simply what lets a chat thread reach into a real terminal — XS gains the depth, kolu gains a front door. Everything social stays in XS.
  • The machine is wherever kolu runs. kolu runs headlessly on any box — your laptop, a server, or a remote sandboxed host. Remote sandboxes (an Incus cluster, another team’s project) are something it naturally supports: a remote host is just another place to dial the same surface.

So the picture is not a tower of dependencies. XS integrates kolu; kolu runs on whatever machine you choose. The arrow is integration one way and execution the other.

The moat: model-agnostic, open, yours

kolu and a chat app divide cleanly. kolu owns the live process, the files, and the durable session. XS owns identity, login, presence, and who-may-write. A foundation that reaches up and grows chat stops being a neutral base any chat app can integrate and becomes one more single-vendor app. Holding that line isn’t caution — it’s the moat.

The moat — our competitive advantage

kolu runs claude, codex, or opencode under any chat app, on infrastructure you control. That is the bet on open standards and open source, and it is exactly what a single-vendor stack can’t match. Claude Tag is one vendor’s model, with the shell and files hidden inside a cloud sandbox you don’t own. kolu keeps the model swappable, the shell and files real, and the host yours — so the chat app on top is a choice, never a lock-in.

What an agent actually is (Andreessen)

Marc Andreessen, on what decades of agent research quietly converged on: “an agent is … a language model, and above that a bash shell … and then a file system, and the state is stored in files,” plus cron — and “every part of that other than the model is something we already completely know.” The kicker: “your agent is now actually independent of the model … you can swap out a different LLM underneath.”

That is kolu’s architecture, line for line: the shell is the interface to every tool (kolu watches it, doesn’t wrap it), the files are the durable state, and the model is the swappable chip (claude · codex · opencode). A chat app that hard-codes one vendor’s model and hides the shell and files inside a cloud sandbox gives up exactly the durable substance kolu keeps.

The seam: observe out raw, act through the coordinator

XS integrates kolu through one seam with two deliberately asymmetric halves: observe flows out raw; act flows in through one door — the coordinator. kolu authenticates nothing: the connection is the trust — an owner-only socket locally, an ssh link to a remote host — so identity, login, and presence stay in XS.

The coordinator is an orchestrator agent running in an ordinary kolu terminal — the same shape kolu’s own development runs on: one agent that provisions worker terminals, dispatches briefs, answers the workers’ questions, and verifies their claims at the tree. Its behavioral contract is the /orchestrator skill: rulings run through the review lenses with named grounding, teardown kills only recorded PIDs, the human merges every PR. The chat bot is a mirror of that coordinator: it binds one thread to that one terminal, renders the coordinator’s reports into the thread, and relays the thread’s messages back in — attributed per XS identity — using the same drive loop the coordinator itself uses on workers.

Surface Half Reuses
the board out · read-only padi’s agent sensors — which agent is working / asking you / just finished (padi-tui wait’s buckets), rendered into the thread on demand with no coordinator hop
attention out · read-only per-terminal urgency through the notify seam — the bot pings the thread instead of the desktopUnprompted posts ride the installed app’s own API: POST /api/apps/chat/postMessage with a conversationId targets a thread, authenticated by the app’s bearer token — the same call pesu answers messages with, so pinging needs no extra machinery.
deep links out a kolu URL to the exact terminal — depth on demand: step in, answer the interactive prompt, debug, in kolu itself
the coordinator bridge in + out one terminal’s screen and input — send a message, wait for the turn to end, read the reply: the identical agent-drives-agent loop kolu already ships

Chat gets no raw act verbs on workers — that absence is the design, not a gap:

  • The write floor dissolves. “At most one writer per terminal” machinery exists only if chat can touch live terminals. With one door, the floor is the coordinator’s inbox: thread messages queue into a conversation and are handled in turn, attributed. Serialization by conversation, not by locks.
  • Guarantees live at the knowing endpoint. The coordinator is the one place that knows campaign state — what is in flight, which merge goes first, what a change must not break — so “who does what next” is decided there, never in a thread reacting to a screen.
  • Discipline is inherited, not re-implemented. Everything the orchestrator contract enforces — claims verified at the tree, grounded rulings, no pattern kills, the human merging — applies to chat traffic automatically, because chat traffic is coordinator traffic.

The same door assists the humans’ own discussion

Because a message to the thread and a message to the coordinator are the same thing, the coordinator is also a participant in the conversation between humans — the teammate shape, not just command-and-control. Several people argue a design in the thread; the coordinator contributes exactly what its contract makes it good at: the claim checked against the actual tree before anyone builds on it, the ruling with its grounding named so the humans can audit the reasoning rather than defer to it, and the running record of what was decided and why. AI-assisted discussion among humans falls out of the coordinator pattern for free — no second bot, no separate “assistant” mode, one attributed inbox.

The XS apps platform, as grounded

The contract pesu builds against — read from the xyne-spaces source (2026-07-13), not its docs, because XS has three separate integration systems that are easy to conflate: the bot catalog (backend-native bots, its own mention/thread semantics), incoming webhooks (URL-embedded-secret message drops), and the apps platform — installed apps with a webhook URL, a JWT token, and a signing secret. pesu is an installed app; only this third system applies.

What an installed app is. Its own per-workspace user (name and avatar from the app record), addressable by @mention, DM-able. Created from the dashboard; the webhook URL, bearer token, and signing secret are per-install credentials.

Events — XS → the app’s webhook URL. One POST per event, {eventType, payload, timestamp}, fired on exactly three chat triggers:

Event Fires when Payload notes
APP_MENTIONED the app is explicitly @mentioned in a channel conversationId (thread), channelId, messageId, sender userId + senderName, body as content (HTML) + cleanContent (text), attachments
DIRECT_MESSAGE every message in a 1:1 DM with the app same shape but no senderName
USER_MENTIONED a human is @mentioned in a channel the app is in observer signal; adds mentionedUserIds

Plain, unmentioned channel messages are never delivered — there is no follow-the-thread for apps (that behavior lives in the bot catalog only). No payload carries a sender email; GET /api/apps/user/info resolves it.

Authentication, both directions, one secret. Deliveries carry X-Xyne-Signature — HMAC-SHA256 (hex) of the raw JSON body with the app’s signing secret; there is no timestamp or replay scheme, so verification is a constant-time HMAC compare and replay is an accepted, recorded risk. The bearer token is a JWT signed HS256 with that same secret, payload {appId, userId}, no expiry — it lives until regenerated.

The app API — the app → XS, Authorization: Bearer. All under /api/apps:

  • POST chat/postMessage — text, markdown, or structured content; target by channelId/channelName, or by conversationId to reply into a thread; posts as the app’s user.
  • POST chat/updateMessage — edit a posted message in place (the growing-reply UX).
  • POST chat/agentProgress — an ephemeral typing/progress indicator.
  • GET chat/channelHistory · GET chat/conversationReplies — read back (catch-up after downtime).
  • POST channel/openDm — open a DM with a user; GET user/info — id → name/email.

Operational facts. Message content caps at 40,000 characters. Event delivery is fire-and-forget: no retries, failures logged server-side only — an app that was down missed those events (the read APIs recover). No effective rate limit is configured on the app API routes; cadence discipline (e.g. ≤1 updateMessage/s) is the app’s own manners.

The first proof: pesu, in the kolu tree

pesu integrates through XS’s apps platform — the shape the installed “kolu” app already has: XS pushes signed events to a webhook URL pesu serves, and pesu talks back through XS’s app API with a bearer token. pesu itself is a small daemon in the kolu source tree (packages/pesu — an app-tier sibling of kolu-server: it imports kolu’s packages, nothing imports it), running beside kolu on the machine you own. Both directions below are grounded in the XS source.

  • In — events, signed. XS POSTs {eventType, payload, timestamp} to pesu’s URL on exactly three chat triggers: APP_MENTIONED (an explicit @kolu in a channel), DIRECT_MESSAGE (every message in a 1:1 DM with the app), and USER_MENTIONED (observer). The payload carries the thread id (conversationId), the channel, the sender’s user id, and the message body as both HTML and plain text. Every delivery is authenticated by X-Xyne-Signature — HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the app’s signing secret — which pesu verifies with a constant-time compare before touching the payload.Three facts to design around, from the XS source: the payload never includes the sender’s email (and the DM payload omits even the display name) — pesu resolves people through GET /api/apps/user/info and caches them; delivery is fire-and-forget with no retries, so pesu answers 200 immediately and works async, and a delivery missed while pesu is down is lost (the read APIs — channelHistory, conversationReplies — allow catch-up); and there is no replay protection on the signature, an accepted risk recorded here.
  • Out — the app API, one bearer token. POST /api/apps/chat/postMessage posts to a channel or — with conversationId — into a thread; updateMessage edits a message in place; agentProgress shows a live typing indicator; channelHistory / conversationReplies read back. This one API is both halves of the mirror: the reply to a message and the unprompted post are the same call — B2 ships no wire B0 doesn’t already have; it is a policy switch (relay the coordinator’s between-message turns), not new machinery.

The one honest UX gap, stated: the apps platform delivers a channel message only on an explicit @mention — the follow-the-thread behavior (replying in a bot’s thread without re-mentioning) exists only in XS’s separate bot-catalog system, not for installed apps. B0’s home is the dedicated kolu channel that already exists: each instruction there @mentions kolu (the DM path works too, ceremony-free, since events for it come free). Two recorded options if the per-message @mention comes to grate: an XS-side feature request for app thread-follow (the right fix), or a pesu-side poller over the dedicated channel’s channelHistory — viable precisely because in that one channel every message is for the coordinator — not built until wanted.

Does the coordinator get chat verbs of its own? No — the coordinator stays chat-unaware, which keeps the mirror agent-CLI-agnostic and the bridge passive. Structured output doesn’t need coordinator agency either: postMessage takes plain text, markdown, and structured payloads, so rendering is pesu’s concern. An MCP face (pesu’s verbs as a @kolu/surface, re-exposed via @kolu/surface-mcp) stays a recorded option whose sole revival condition is a coordinator demonstrably needing to initiate a chat action the transcript mirror cannot express.

Each phase is one PR, end to end — it ships nothing that isn’t consumed within it (the padi plan’s law, held here). Every PR below is a complete, usable product on its own.

B0 — the round trip

B0· the bridge daemon — a chat-driven coordinator over the installed app▶ do next

What you see: in the dedicated kolu channel, “@kolu ‹ask›” talks to the coordinator — your message lands in its terminal prefixed with your name; the answer appears in the thread as one message that grows while it works, with a typing indicator during the turn. (DMing the app works identically, with no @ needed.) B0 is single-operator by design: a configured allowlist of one — srid — and a message from anyone else gets a one-line visible decline, never silence and never a relayed turn. Multi-operator attribution is already built into the write-in (every message carries its sender), so widening later is a config change, not a code change.

The turn, end to end: verify X-Xyne-Signature (constant-time) → 200 immediately → enqueue on the FIFO inbox (the write floor — one turn in flight, ever) → resolve the coordinator terminal by title via the kaval client (ids re-key across kaval restarts; titles survive) → resolve the sender via user/info (cached) → attributed two-step write-in, snapshot-verified → agentProgress on → as the reply grows in the coordinator’s transcript, read it through the shipped loaders (kolu-claude-code / kolu-codex / kolu-grok / kolu-opencode, dispatched on the agent kind padi publishes — the same dispatch padi/transcript.ts does, so B0 is model-agnostic on day one) → postMessage once, then updateMessage at a civil cadence so the thread shows one growing message → the turn-end bucket flips → final update, typing off. A fault posts as a visible reply — never silence. Replies split at XS’s 40,000-character message cap.

The code tree (no transcript module — the loaders already exist):

packages/pesu/src/
  bin.ts            # entry: config → webhook server + turn engine
  config.ts         # XS base URL · listen port · coordinator title ·
                    #   env NAMES for the signing secret + bearer token
  webhook.ts        # the receiver: HMAC verify, event parse, immediate 200
  xyneApi.ts        # the bearer client: postMessage · updateMessage ·
                    #   agentProgress · user/info (+ user cache)
  inbox.ts          # the FIFO turn queue — the write floor
  coordinator.ts    # terminal-by-title · attributed write-in · turn-end via
                    #   padi's buckets · reply text via the loaders
  attribution.ts    # "from Sridhar: " prefix formatting

Hard requirements, in the PR: a stable public URL for the webhook — the recommended shape for a home-manager host: pesu binds 127.0.0.1:<port> as a systemd user service, fronted by Tailscale Funnel (tailscale funnel), which gives a stable https://<host>.<tailnet>.ts.net hostname with TLS terminated by tailscaled — no extra daemon, survives restarts, and the hostname registered in XS never changes (a cloudflared named tunnel is the fallback if Funnel is unavailable; quick-tunnels rotate their hostname per run and silently orphan the registration). Secrets reach pesu only as environment variables — never the repo, the PR, logs, or an agent transcript; the sender allowlist rejects non-operators visibly; a forged-signature request is rejected (pinned by a test); a coordinator-busy message queues and answers in order.

B2 — the live mirror

B2· unprompted posts over the same app API — the thread becomes the campaign feed○ todo
needs ← B0

What you see: the thread updates on its own. A worker finishes and the coordinator’s report appears; a ruling goes out and you read it as it happens; an agent needs a human and the thread gets pinged — each post carrying a link that opens the exact terminal in kolu when you want the depth. Mechanically this is B0’s postMessage with a conversationId and the transcript relay switched on for between-message turns — no new wire, which is why it is the roadmap’s smallest PR.

The discussion-assist patterns — the coordinator contributing grounded answers to a debate between humans — are coordinator behavior, the /orchestrator skill’s territory, and deliberately not a pesu PR.

The milestone is concrete: run kolu’s own development from a thread (B0 + B1).

The target user story, end to end — here replaying a real merged change, PR #1544, which made session export a lightweight chat log: start an agent from a thread, watch it work, get screenshot evidence, jump into the live terminal to try it, then take the PR to green and merge — all without leaving chat. The first milestone lights up the observe half (the stream and the evidence); attaching to test and merging from chat ride the act-in verbs that follow.

The call

kolu is the foundation a chat app integrates — real terminals, durable sessions, an honest read, and one disciplined door for writes: the coordinator. XS owns identity; kolu owns the substance; the coordinator owns the discipline — and lends it to the humans’ own discussion. Build the bridge, prove it with the pesu bot running kolu’s own development in the open, and let any chat app be the front door.
